Manual

Everything the SMK-37 Pro does under Tonitor. New here? Start with Playing it; to install, see Install.

Not a groovebox

No tempo, no steps, no patterns, no drum kit.

Tonitor is for sound heard for itself: texture, grain, movement and slow transformation. You play drones, gestures and textures, layer them, loop them freely out of time with one another, and shape them while they play. It suits acousmatic and electroacoustic work as much as live ambient music, dark ambient above all.

Playing it

Tonitor turns the SMK-37 Pro into six tracks. Each track has its own engine and sound, its own level, pan, filter, granulator, crush and distortion, and its own sends to a master delay and a master reverb. You choose a track on the top row of pads and play it on the keys. The other tracks go on sounding: held notes, latched notes, loops and sequencers keep playing while you choose and play another track.

The tracks start on FM, ANIMA, CALIGULA, HIVE, DRUID and BAYAREA (tracks 1 to 6), with a new sound each, on the OPEN path, in C MAJOR. Each track has a colour: 1 yellow, 2 cyan, 3 pink, 4 green, 5 orange, 6 lilac.

The keys

All 37 keys play. With a scale chosen, every key, black or white, plays the next step of the scale, up from the root on the lowest key. The keyboard is one continuous run of the scale: a seven-note scale spans a little over five octaves. With CHROMATIC, the keyboard plays as printed, C3 to C6.

Each track's octave 0 places the 37 keys for the scale's length. A twelve-note scale (CHROMATIC) starts at C3. A seven- or eight-note scale starts an octave lower. A five- or six-note scale starts two octaves lower. OCTAVE− and OCTAVE+ move the chosen track from there, as far as every key stays in MIDI's range. A change of scale or root brings each track's octave back into range if it has to.

The keys answer velocity. GLOBAL SETUP's VELOCITY section sets the curve and the range (see Global setup and MIDI). The softest note a key plays is velocity 16, so a light touch is never lost on a sound that answers velocity strongly. A strike slower than 150 ms is taken as one of 60 ms.

Voices come from one pool of twelve shared by all the tracks (CALIGULA and RUSSOLO are one organism a track, outside the pool). A note takes a free voice, so a track has as many as its notes need, and a new note never cuts the release of the one before while voices are free. A key let go ends its note on the track it was played on, so a held note keeps sounding while you choose and play another track. See Voices and load.

Generative paths

Each track has a path that leans what HOME draws, on every engine. A path changes nothing already playing: it shapes the next sounds drawn on that track. Pads 7 and 8 show the chosen track's path.

PathPadLeans towards
AMBIENT7sounds for ambient and dark ambient: ethereal, melodic, often melancholic. FM favours drones, beating spectra (SPECTRE), voices (CHOIR), bowed, hollow and tidal tones, mallets, LADDER, REVERSE and CREEP, never BRUIT, IMPACT, FRICTION, SHARDS, STATIC or GLITCH; then softer attacks, long tails, darker modulators, slow LFOs, no sirens, often an octave down. ANIMA draws mostly HAZE, GOLDEN, VOYAGE, TIDE, CHOIR, BOWL, FOG and DRIFT, with a darker tone, more space, a slower hand and long releases. CALIGULA draws SPORE, VEIL and LITANY most; tuned on roots, fifths, octaves and unisons; slow swells and a slower hand. RUSSOLO draws CHORD most, then DUST, CRACKLE, BLIPS, WALK and WANDER, clean and slow. DRUID favours BOWED, HARP, DRONE, BELL and BOWL with long decays. BAYAREA favours BONGO, CHIME, SWELL and DRONE. HIVE favours PAD, DRONE, WASH, SPECTRA and TIDES, slower and darker
EXPERIMENTAL8sounds for electroacoustic and acousmatic music: edgier, gnarlier. FM favours WARP and GLITCH most, then bruits, frictions, shards, static, SHAPER and CLANG, brighter, bent more often, never SPECTRE, CHOIR, BOWED or TIDE. ANIMA draws mostly GRIT, SWARM, SHARDS, MACHINE, BITS and HOWL, and makes them wild. CALIGULA draws WIRE, THORN, HIVE and RUST most; clusters and tritones; sharper and more driven. RUSSOLO draws NOR, XOR, CLANG, BEND and QUAD most, crushed and abrupt. DRUID favours RATTLE and PLATE with shorter decays. BAYAREA favours PLUCK and FOLDED with more drive and folding. HIVE favours STAB, CLUSTER, METAL, GROUND and AIR, with more noise and drive
OPENneither litevery family, kind and species alike. Every track starts here

The engines section gives each engine's families and what the paths do to them. Sessions keep each track's path, and the path each of its sounds was drawn on.

Macros

Press MACRO (lit while on) and the eight knobs stop being the track's mix and effects: they become eight macros that reshape the chosen track's sound while it plays, under a held note. The band under the engine says EDIT in red as long as the macros are on. Press MACRO again to give the knobs back.

Each macro turns from the middle, which is the sound as HOME drew it; either way transforms it. Each answers early in its turn (a quarter of the way gives half the change). While a knob turns, the whole screen is its dial, with the macro's name for this sound, the track and how far it is turned (+40 %, −25 %, AS DRAWN).

Envelope

Press FADER BANK (lit while the page is up) to open the ENVELOPE page; press it again, or a track pad, to close it. The page shows ENVELOPE and the track's number, the amplitude envelope of the chosen track's sound drawn as a curve, and ATTACK, DECAY, SUSTAIN and RELEASE with their values.

As HOME drew the sound, the page reads the sound's own envelope and says AS DRAWN (in grey): for FM, the envelope of the loudest carrier; for CALIGULA, the average of its pairs' attacks and releases. CALIGULA and RUSSOLO have no decay or sustain stage (shown as 5 ms and 100 %).

KnobRange
K3ATTACK1 ms – 10 s
K4DECAY5 ms – 10 s
K5SUSTAIN0–100 %
K6RELEASE5 ms – 20 s

The times are on logarithmic scales. K1 and K2 stay the track's level and pan. The value just turned is drawn black on white for a moment.

The first turn starts from the values shown and replaces the sound's own amplitude envelope with the track's: the attack is linear, the decay and release are exponential, the release ending 60 dB down. FM's carrier envelopes and ANIMA's envelope are then held at full; CALIGULA and RUSSOLO are kept playing through the release and then let go. Once the track's envelope is in use, turning the knobs also changes the notes that sound.

HOME (a new sound) or loading a preset gives the sound's own envelope back. Each track keeps an envelope for each of its eight engines. Sessions store them and copying a track copies them; presets do not.

The bottom row of pads

The bottom row of pads (9 to 16) plays no notes. It shows the page of the button that opened it, one page at a time: opening another replaces it. The pages stay up while you choose other tracks; they act on the chosen track.

Chords

With chord mode on for a track, each key plays three notes: its own note and two more of the same scale. Every chord stays in the scale, and its quality (major, minor, diminished) is the scale's at that degree.

Press CHORD to turn the chosen track's chord mode on or off (CHORD lit while on). The screen says the form, or CHORDS OFF. While chord mode is on, CHO shows at the top left of the screen, with the form's abbreviation under it in grey.

Hold CHORD (0.6 s) to put the forms on the bottom row of pads; chord mode comes on with them. Press a pad to choose a form (its name shows on the screen). Hold CHORD again to free the pads. Turning chord mode off, or choosing a track whose chord mode is off, takes the forms off the pads.

PadFormSteps of the scaleScreen
9TRIAD0, 2, 4TRIroot, third, fifth (the start)
10INV 12, 4, 7IN1first inversion: the third at the bottom, the root an octave up
11INV 2−3, 0, 2IN2second inversion: the fifth below the root
12SUS20, 1, 4SU2the third replaced by the second
13SUS40, 3, 4SU4the third replaced by the fourth
14OPEN0, 4, 9OPNroot, fifth, and the third an octave up
15FOURTHS0, 3, 64THstacked fourths
16FIFTHS0, 4, 85THstacked fifths

One chord sounds at a time on a track: a new key lets the one before go. Chords follow the loops' moves along the scale like single notes, latch with SHIFT (all three notes), are recorded by the loopers as three notes, and apply to BALLSY's and BRICKLAYER's notes as to keys. Sessions keep chord mode, its form and the chords latched; copying a track copies its chord mode.

Latched keys

A latched note sounds on after you let go of its key.

  • SHIFT held, then a key: the note latches at once.
  • Keys held, then SHIFT: the keys held latch.
  • A latched key pressed alone: it is struck again and stays latched. A struck sound that has faded, or a note that was cut, sounds again.
  • SHIFT + a latched key: that latch is let go; its note ends as a released key's would.
  • SHIFT tapped twice (within 0.35 s): every latched note on every track is let go (LATCH OFF).

Latches belong to the track they were made on. On another track the same keys play as usual, so a drone can be left on one track while you play another. A latched note keeps the velocity it was struck at, also when it is moved along the scale. Latched notes are never taken by a new note and never cut by the load protection (see Voices and load). Sessions keep the latches.

The loopers

Every track has its own looper of up to eight loops, and they are all free: no tempo, no grid, no quantising, not even between a track's own loops. Each overdub is a loop of its own, as long as you made it, going round in its own length over the others, so they drift in and out of phase. Each plays back what was played, to 0.73 ms, with each note's velocity (in 16 steps).

  • Press REC to arm a new loop: REC blinks and the band under the engine flashes ARMED and the loop's number in red. Press REC again before playing to disarm it.
  • The first note you play starts the recording: REC lights and the band shows REC and the number, white on red.
  • Press REC again to end it: the loop is exactly as long as from that first note to this press. It plays at once, round and round (LOOP n). If the track's loops were stopped, they all start again with it.
  • Press REC again while it plays to overdub: the same again, a new loop over the others.
  • The ninth is refused: the screen says 8 LOOPS.
  • REC held (1 s) empties the track's looper, all its loops (LOOP n / EMPTY). Emptying returns the loops to forwards, normal speed and VARY off, and takes away the track's own move along the scale.

A loop can last up to 12.7 minutes; it closes there by itself. A track's loops hold about 500 notes between them. A note still held when REC closes the loop is tied over its end: it sounds on unbroken as the loop goes round, so a drone stays one long note.

The keys go on playing the track over its loops, and the loops' notes and the keys' never cut each other's notes off. The looper records only what is played on the keys (and MIDI in): BALLSY's, BRICKLAYER's and REACT's notes are never recorded.

PLAY stops the chosen track's loops, or plays them again, each from its start. PLAY is lit while they play.

Bringing loops in and out. Hold PLAY (0.6 s; it does not start or stop anything): the chosen track's loops appear on the bottom row of pads, loop 1 (the first one recorded) on pad 9, each overdub on the next. Press a pad to take its loop out (its notes stop, the others go on) or to bring it back in: it comes in at once, from its start. While PLAY is held, the screen shows the loops (in the track's colour: in; a grey frame: out), and the keys from the lowest one up do the same as the pads: the lowest white key loop 1, the next white key loop 2, and so on. The pads stay up after you let go of PLAY; hold PLAY again to free them. With the loops stopped, this chooses which will play: take out all but one, press PLAY, and only that one starts; then bring the others in, one by one. Every loop is in when recorded. Sessions keep which loops are out.

Moving the loops along the scale. Hold SHIFT and press OCTAVE+ or OCTAVE−: every loop of every track moves one step of the chosen scale up or down, so each loop keeps its shape within the scale. Latched notes and the sequencers move with them. The notes sounding move at once, at the velocity they sounded at. The screen shows how far they are moved (TRANSP +2, TRANSP −1, TRANSP 0), up to two octaves of the scale either way. Choosing another scale or root while they are moved walks the new one. The keys move with them: on a track, they play the scale moved as far as that track's loops are, so what you add fits what is there, and an overdub recorded while the loops are moved plays back as you played it. MIDI notes are not moved. Sessions keep the move.

One track along the scale. Hold SHIFT, hold a track's pad, and press OCTAVE+ or OCTAVE−: only that track's loops, latched notes and sequencer move, a step of the scale at a time (TRANSP T3 +2). It adds to the move of all the loops. Holding the track's pad with SHIFT down never copies it. Emptying a track's loops takes its own move away; copying a track takes it along; sessions keep it.

Loop options

Press LOOP to put the chosen track's loop options on the bottom row of pads (LOOP lit; LOOP PADS); press it again to free the pads. Each pad is lit while its option is on and dim while off. The options apply to all the track's loops together, each within its own length.

PadOption
9REVERSEthe loops play backwards: each note starts where it ended and ends where it started
10PENDULUMforwards to the end of each loop, backwards to its start, and so on
11RANDOMeach time the next note is due (and at the loop's end), the loop jumps to a note of it drawn at random and goes on from there. Each note keeps its length and the time to the note that followed it; notes struck together stay together; the notes sounding are let go at each jump
12STUTTEReach loop wanders about its eighths: at the end of each eighth the next is drawn: the same again, the one before, the next (twice as likely) or the one after it. What sounds is let go at each jump. Not with RANDOM
13CLIMB DOWNeach pass a step of the scale lower, round an octave of the scale and back to where it began
14CLIMB UPeach pass a step of the scale higher, round an octave of the scale
15HALFthe loops take twice as long (the pitch does not change)
16DOUBLEthe loops take half as long

REVERSE, PENDULUM and RANDOM exclude each other (none lit: forwards), as do HALF and DOUBLE (none lit: normal speed); pressing the lit pad again goes back. CLIMB DOWN and CLIMB UP exclude each other. STUTTER and the climbs are each on or off. All of them combine with the direction and the speed. The climb moves on each time the track's first playing loop comes round; its sounding notes are let go then, and a tied note is struck again.

Changing the direction while a loop plays continues from where it is. An overdub recorded at half or double speed, or while the loops play backwards, is stored so that it plays back as it was played. Sessions keep the options; copying a track copies them. The screen names each change (REVERSE, FORWARD, HALF SPEED, NORMAL SPEED, STUTTER, STUTTER OFF, CLIMB UP, CLIMB OFF).

VARY

SHIFT + REC turns the chosen track's loops' VARY on or off (VARY, VARY OFF; VAR at the top right of the screen while on). Each note the loops play gets a random level (from −10 dB to full) and a random length (50 ms to 1.5 s) instead of the recorded one. Now and then, at odds of its own, a note is changed or joined:

  • dropped this time round (5 %);
  • late by 5–40 ms (25 %);
  • an octave up or down (8 %);
  • replaced or joined by a note a step or two of the scale away, or a fifth (8 %);
  • preceded by a grace note a step away (4 %);
  • struck 2–4 times quickly (4 %);
  • joined by a third or fifth above (10 %);
  • echoed 1–4 times 120–400 ms apart, each quieter, sometimes climbing or falling a step each time (15 %);
  • the notes of a chord strummed 20–60 ms apart (12 %).

Every note stays in the scale. The loops' pace is no longer steady either: it rises and falls slowly, and every few seconds on average it halts for a moment and resumes, bursts to 2–3 times for a moment, grinds to a stop and snaps back, or climbs to 2–2.5 times and drops suddenly (not while REC records). VARY applies to all the track's loops. Sessions keep it; emptying the loops turns it off.

PLAY, the sequencers and the looper

A track has one sequencer at a time: while its BALLSY is on, BRICKLAYER says NOT ALLOWED and changes nothing, and the other way round. The looper works beside either.

A sequencer turned on waits for PLAY. On the sequencer's page, PLAY starts and stops it (PLAY or STOP on the screen), and PLAY blinks while it plays. While the chosen track's sequencer plays, PLAY blinks on every page and stops it from there. When no sequencer of the chosen track plays and its page is down, PLAY is the looper's. So you can put a sequencer's page down, record loops over it from the keys, and start and stop the loops with PLAY. SHIFT + PLAY starts or stops every loop and sequencer of every track together.

The sequencers' notes play as a key's would: in the scale, with the loops' moves along the scale and chord mode. The looper does not record them. REACT, SHADOW and ARP hear them when they play on the guide track.

BALLSY

BALLSY turns on a physics sequencer of bouncing balls for the chosen track and shows its page; BALLSY is lit while it is on and blinks while it plays. Press BALLSY again to turn it off. The balls wait in the middle until PLAY (on their page) starts them; PLAY again holds them still where they are (their notes let go), and PLAY once more moves them on from there. Each track has its own, and they run at the same time.

Hold BALLSY (0.6 s) while it is on to put its page down or up. With the page down the balls keep playing, and the knobs, the screen and the other pages work as usual. A track pad or another page also puts it down.

One to eight balls move in a box on the screen. Each time a ball hits a wall, it plays a note on the track. Each note's length (50 ms to 1.5 s) and level (from −10 dB to full) are drawn at random; the level applies to FM, ANIMA, DRUID, BAYAREA and HIVE (CALIGULA and RUSSOLO play at their own level). Each bounce changes the ball's angle at random by up to 12°, kept between 15° and 75° from the walls, so the paths change and every wall is reached. Each wall holds the notes of the scale, one segment a step, and the segment hit lights up. The pitch rises clockwise all the way round, one octave a wall:

WallOctave (at the start)Direction of rising pitch
bottom−1 (the octave below the keyboard's)right to left
left0 (the keyboard's)upwards
top+1left to right
right+2downwards

While the page is up, K3–K6 control the balls (K1 and K2 stay level and pan):

Knob
K3the number of balls, 1–8; new ones start from the middle in a random direction
K4speed, 0–100 (from 0.08 to 2.4 box widths a second)
K5the octaves of the four walls, moved together by one octave a click
K6instability, 0–100 (0 at the start): each ball gets a wind of its own, two values that wander at random. One scales its speed, up to 8 times faster or slower at 100, so a ball can nearly stop and then rush on; the other turns it, up to half a turn a second. Occasional gusts change its direction by up to 60°. At 0 the pace is steady and the paths straight

The screen shows the box, the walls' segments in the track's colour and the balls; the line above shows the number of balls, or the value just turned. Sessions store each track's balls and whether they are on and playing; copying a track copies them.

BRICKLAYER

BRICKLAYER turns on a step sequencer built a note at a time, for the chosen track, and shows its page; BRICKLAYER is lit while it is on and blinks while it plays. A short press while it is on turns it off (its notes are kept). It waits for PLAY (on its page), which starts it from its first step and, pressed again, stops it (its notes let go). Notes can be entered whether it plays or not. Each track has its own.

Hold BRICKLAYER (0.6 s) to put its options on the bottom row of pads (BRICKS PADS); if it was off, it comes on with them, its page up. Hold it again to free the pads.

On its page, REC is the entry, not the looper:

Gesture
RECentry on or off (REC stays lit while it is on)
a key, entry onits note is added at the end of the sequence (and sounds)
SHIFT + a key, entry onthat note is taken out, wherever it is
SHIFT + RECthe last note added is taken out (LAST OUT)
REC held (1 s)the sequence is emptied (BRICKS / EMPTY)

The notes play in the order they were added, spread over the sequence's length as evenly as possible (a Euclidean rhythm, the first note on the first step: 3 notes in 8 steps fall on steps 1, 4 and 7). Notes are kept as steps of the scale, so they follow the moves along the scale, the scale and the root, as latched notes do. Chord mode applies to them as to keys. Up to 32 notes.

Knob
K3LENGTH: steps, from the number of notes up to 32
K4RATE: 0.5–16 steps a second
K5HARMONY: how often a note becomes a diad (a third or a fifth above) or a triad
K6VARIATION: each note's level (down to −12 dB) and length (from a quarter to twice the usual) spread at random; the pace wanders (from half to twice the rate), and now and then stops for a moment or rushes; as likely as the knob says, a note stutters (struck 2–4 times within its step), the last 2–4 steps are played again (beat repeat), a note echoes 1–3 times, quieter, or an empty step plays a quiet ghost note from the sequence. At 0: a steady level and length, a steady pace

BRICKLAYER's options on pads 9–16 are laid out as the loops' and work the same way on its steps:

PadOption
9REVERSEthe steps backwards
10PENDULUMforwards and backwards in turn
11RANDOMa step drawn at random each time
12STUTTERit wanders: the same step again, the one before, the next or the one after it
13CLIMB DOWNa step of the scale lower after each run of its steps, round an octave of the scale
14CLIMB UPa step higher after each run of its steps
15HALFhalf speed
16DOUBLEdouble speed

With BRICKLAYER's page up, LOOP's pads set BRICKLAYER's options too, all eight: its direction, STUTTER, the climbs and its speed, as BRICKLAYER's own pads do.

The screen shows the steps as cells, eight to a row (up to four rows): a note's cell filled in the track's colour, an empty one as an outline, the step being played in white. The line above shows the notes and the steps (3 IN 8), REC and the number of notes while entering, or the value just turned. Each note lasts 70 % of its step (VARIATION spreads it). Sessions store each track's sequence, settings and options; copying a track copies them.

REACT, SHADOW and ARP

In these three modes the other tracks play along with the one you play. The chosen track is the guide. The tracks you take in listen to everything the guide sounds (its keys, latches, chords, MIDI in, loops, BALLSY and BRICKLAYER) and play their own sounds in answer, in the scale. Choosing another track makes it the guide.

  • SHIFT + FADER BANK turns the mode on or off at once (REACT, REACT OFF; SHADOW, SHADOW OFF; ARP, ARP OFF). FADER BANK blinks slowly while it is on.
  • FADER BANK held (0.6 s) puts its page up, with its pads on the bottom row. Held again while the page is up, both go down. A track pad also puts the page down; the mode goes on running, and its pads stay up.
  • On the page, < and > choose the mode: REACT, SHADOW or ARP. Changing the mode lets go of the notes the tracks are playing.
  • On the pads, pads 9–14 are tracks 1–6. Press a pad to take that track in or out (2 IN, 2 OUT): lit in the mode's colour while in, dim while out. At first no track is in. The guide's pad is dark; pressed, it lights red for a moment and the screen says GUIDE TRACK (a track cannot follow itself).
  • K1 and K2 stay the guide's level and pan. K3–K6 (ARP: K3–K8) set the mode's values, 0–100.

The page shows the mode's name (in its colour while on, grey while off), the name of the knob turned last, its value large, and a bar for each knob. REACT is sea green, SHADOW pale blue, ARP lime.

The tracks taken in play their notes as a sequencer's: the looper does not record them, and they never play on the guide. When the guide stops, they stop. The modes, the tracks taken in and their values are not kept in sessions.

REACT

REACT improvises from a memory of everything the guide plays: its last 128 events (notes or chords), with their levels, lengths and the gaps before them, kept as steps of the scale. After François Pachet's Continuator, IRCAM's OMax and Somax, and George Lewis's Voyager.

Each track taken in improvises from that memory. From the event it played last, it goes on as the guide once went on, or jumps to another place in the memory where the guide played the same intervals (and rhythm), and goes on from there. So its lines are the guide's own, recombined: new phrases in the guide's style, never a pattern of its own. Its rhythm is the guide's, slowed or quickened by its own factor. Each choice is weighed by how it fits the harmony now (what the guide holds, and the pitch classes it played lately), and its notes are moved a third if that fits better. Every note is kept in the scale. When the guide's harmony moves, a long note that no longer fits lets go.

At each of the guide's phrases, and every 6 to 9 seconds of unbroken playing, the tracks regroup. Each takes a way to play, suited to its sound (a texture such as CALIGULA, RUSSOLO, drones and washes plays only slow, low, single notes), and a register of its own:

Way
FOLLOWSwith the guide, as fast or half as fast, its harmony followed closely
CONTRASTSagainst it: slow and long under a busy guide, moving under one holding long chords; the other side of the keyboard, softer
ECHOESthe guide's line a few events behind, a third, a sixth or an octave away; at a rest, the rest of it
ANSWERSin the guide's rest: its phrase continued as the guide might have, until the guide plays again
RESTSsits out this time
Knob
K3DENSITYhow much they play: how often a track sounds, how long it waits (from twice to half the guide's gaps), how many sit out
K4COMPLEXITYlow: single notes in plain rhythms; high: harmonised notes (a third or a sixth under), notes moved further along the scale, steps split in two or three, notes pushed off the beat, threes against twos
K5CONTINUITYlow: they jump about the guide's memory, recombining it; high: they keep to its phrases as played
K6SPREADhow far from the guide's register: low, around its hands; high, from deep bass to high air

They start at DENSITY 50, COMPLEXITY 40, CONTINUITY 60, SPREAD 40. After a long silence of the guide, the tracks let go and wait.

SHADOW

The tracks taken in shadow what the guide sounds, each from its own distance behind, at its own pace. Now and then a shadow goes backwards or to and fro, rests and comes in again, its rhythm loosened, moved along the scale.

Knob
K3DELAYhow far behind: from right behind (a note or two) to 15 s, each shadow at its own distance
K4DRIFThow far each one's pace strays from the guide's: from a little loose to half, two thirds, three quarters, one and a third, one and a half or twice, in and out of step
K5VARIATIONhow often each changes its way: low, forwards and steady for long; high, backwards, to and fro, resting and coming in again, notes late, left out or struck twice
K6TRANSPOSEhow far it is moved: low, as played (or an octave); high, a third, a fourth, a fifth or a sixth away

They start at DELAY 30, DRIFT 30, VARIATION 40, TRANSPOSE 30.

ARP

The tracks taken in break the guide's chord into arpeggios, each at its own pace, its own way and in its own octaves, and follow the chord as it changes. The chord is what the guide holds (a finger lifted, a note less); let go, the last chord goes on until the guide has been silent a while. A single note is arpeggiated over its octaves. A new chord, once it has stood 90 ms, is taken by each track at its next step, from the start of its pattern: never between two of its notes, the pulse unbroken. From silence, the first chord starts them at once. Textures arpeggiate four times slower. The page shows K3–K8 in two rows of three.

Knob
K3RATEthe pace: a step every 2 s (0) to every 62 ms (100), steady
K4RELATIONhow the tracks' paces relate: all one at 0; higher, twice, half, three in two, two in three, four in three, three times as fast, each track its own, interlocking
K5MOTIONwhich way: all up at 0; higher, each its own (down, up and down, down and up, the order played, from the outside in, from the middle out, at random), the second against the first; high, a track turns another way now and then
K6MUTATEhow much a pattern changes as it repeats: fixed at 0; higher, steps swapped, a rest, a step struck again, the pattern turned
K7RANGEhow many octaves each spans, 1 to 4, and how far apart the tracks sit
K8CHANCEtight at 0; higher, steps left out and steps struck twice

They start at RATE 50, RELATION 40, MOTION 40, MUTATE 20, RANGE 30, CHANCE 10.

Copying a track

Hold a track's pad until the screen flashes COPIED / TRACK n: the track is on the clipboard, and its pad blinks. Choose another track and hold its pad until PASTED / TRACK n: it now has the copied track's tone, sequencers and loops. The clipboard is then empty: the next hold copies again. Holding the copied track's own pad again copies it again (as it is now), pasting nothing.

What is copied: the tone (the engine, the sounds of all eight engines with their macros and envelopes, the filter, the granulator, the crush, the distortion, the delay and reverb sends, the octave, the path, the modulation and the chord mode), BALLSY and BRICKLAYER with their settings, and all the loops with their options and VARY, every overdub, those taken out still out. The copy is taken when you hold the pad: what the track does afterwards is not pasted. The track pasted onto keeps its level and pan; whatever it had before is replaced, and its latched notes are let go. The clipboard is kept in the flash beside the sessions (writing it may hush the audio for a moment); it is emptied when the keyboard is switched off.

The wheels and the master

The pitch wheel bends the chosen track up to 2 semitones either way. Every engine bends. The mod wheel adds a vibrato (5.5 Hz, up to 0.4 semitone) and pushes the first macro of the sound up, up to its full turn. Both act on the chosen track only; choosing another track lets go of them on the one left. The wheels calibrate themselves: the pitch wheel's rest is taken at power-on.

Fader 4 (the rightmost) is the master level. It sets what reaches the headphones and the outputs, not the USB audio (see USB audio).

The screen

The screen is made for low vision: few words, very large type, high contrast.

From top to bottom, the track view shows:

  • the track number, very large, in the track's colour; at the top left CHO and the chord form while chord mode is on; at the top right the battery (three bars green, two green, one amber, one red when low; a white bolt on a computer's USB power, when the reading is the supply's) and the track's octave to its left (+1, −2; nothing at 0), with VAR under them while the loops VARY;
  • the track's engine, in white;
  • the family of its sound, in the track's colour. When something changes (NEW, OCT +1, LOOP 2), a black-on-white message replaces it for a moment. While the looper is armed this band flashes ARMED and the loop's number in red; while it records it shows REC and the number, white on red. While MACRO is on it says EDIT in red;
  • the track's level meter: a bar filling from the left in the track's colour as it sounds (−48 to +6 dB), and a white mark at the level K1 sets (red at the left when the track is off);
  • at the very bottom, the track's pan: a block in its colour on a line from left to right, with a tick at the middle.

K3 to K8 (filter, granulator, crush, distortion, delay send, reverb send) each show, while they turn and for a second after, a full-screen dial: the knob's name and the track, an arc from 7 to 5 o'clock lit in the track's colour, a white pointer, and in large type what it does (LP 1.2 KHZ, DARK 40, BITS 6.5, SEND 40). The macros show the same dial. K1 and K2 say their value in the message band.

Saving, loading, emptying a looper, copying and pasting flash the whole screen for 1.5 s. The pages (SCALE, ENVELOPE, DELAY, REVERB, MOD, SNAPSHOTS, SESSIONS, PRESETS, GLOBAL SETUP, BALLSY, BRICKLAYER, the loops while PLAY is held, REACT) each take the whole screen and are described in their sections. On every page, the value just turned is drawn black on white for a moment.

If the chip's second core did not start, the screen says 1 CORE for a few seconds: the instrument plays, with half the room for voices.

Scales

One scale and root for the whole keyboard, saved with the session; C MAJOR at the start. Press SCALE to open the SCALE page: K1 chooses the root (C to B, round the octave), K2 the scale. The page shows SCALE, the root very large, and the scale's name under it; what you just turned is drawn black on white for a moment. SCALE again, or a track pad, goes back.

The root sits on the lowest key and the scale climbs from there across all 37 keys, black keys included (see The keys for where each scale starts).

ScaleSteps
MAJOR0 2 4 5 7 9 11
MINOR NATURAL0 2 3 5 7 8 10
MINOR HARMONIC0 2 3 5 7 8 11
MINOR MELODIC0 2 3 5 7 9 11
DORIAN0 2 3 5 7 9 10
MINOR PENTA0 3 5 7 10
WHOLE TONE0 2 4 6 8 10
ENIGMATIC0 1 4 6 8 10 11
JAPANESE IN0 1 5 7 8: the in (miyako-bushi) scale of the koto and shakuhachi
PHRYGIAN0 1 3 5 7 8 10
LYDIAN0 2 4 6 7 9 11
MIXOLYDIAN0 2 4 5 7 9 10
LOCRIAN0 1 3 5 6 8 10
MAJOR PENTA0 2 4 7 9
BLUES0 3 5 6 7 10
HUNGARIAN MINOR0 2 3 6 7 8 11
DOUBLE HARMONIC0 1 4 5 7 8 11 (also called Byzantine)
PHRYGIAN DOMINANT0 1 4 5 7 8 10: the fifth mode of the harmonic minor
JAPANESE HIRAJOSHI0 2 3 7 8

The screen splits the longer names over two lines (MIXO- LYDIAN, HUNGAR- IAN MINOR, OCTA- TONIC, PROME- THEUS, CHROMA- TIC) rather than squeezing the letters together. MIDI notes are not quantised to the scale.

Presets

Each engine has 64 presets, P1 to P64, for the sounds you want to keep and bring back on any track. Hold SHIFT and press SCALE: the PRESETS page of the chosen track's engine opens (the engine's name over the slots), four slots a page. < and > step through them; a slot holding a sound shows its number in red and the sound's family numbered among that engine's presets of the family, in the order of the slots (BRASS 1, BRASS 2, STRINGS 1); an empty one EMPTY in grey. SHIFT + SCALE again, or a track pad, goes back.

  • SCALE held (0.8 s), or SAVE held, saves the track's sound into the slot chosen. Over a sound already there it asks OVERWRITE? first, on NO until > turns it to YES (< back to NO); SCALE (or SAVE) answers.
  • SCALE pressed, or SAVE pressed, loads the slot chosen into the track (which crossfades to it, as to a new sound) and goes back to playing. An empty slot says EMPTY.

A preset keeps what draws the sound again exactly (its seed, its family, its path and the generation of the generators that drew it), its level and its eight macros. A sound chosen by family (SHIFT + < / >, SHIFT + HOME) comes back the same from a preset or a session. It does not keep the track's envelope: a preset loads with the sound's own. A preset loaded draws the same modulation as HOME would with that sound. Saving erases flash, which silences the audio for a moment.

Snapshots

A snapshot is the state of the machine at one moment. Each session holds 16 of them, one on each pad.

Press SAVE (lit while the page is up): the SNAPSHOTS page opens, 16 boxes in two rows of eight, as the pads. A filled box holds a snapshot; the one last stored or recalled is white. While the page is up, the 16 pads are the snapshots, the top row 1 to 8 and the bottom row 9 to 16: they choose no track and no path. A pad holding a snapshot glows; the one last stored or recalled is lit; an empty pad is dark.

ToDo this
Recall a snapshotpress and release its pad
Store the current statehold its pad 0.8 s, or frame it with < and > and hold SAVE
Empty a snapshothold SHIFT and hold its pad 0.8 s
Set the morph time (0 to 30 s)K3
Leave the pageSAVE again

The keys go on playing while the page is up, and K1 and K2 stay the track's level and pan.

What a snapshot holds. The whole state of the machine. For each track: the engine it plays; the sound on every one of its eight engines, each with its eight macros and its envelope; level, pan, reverb and delay sends, filter, granulator, crush, distortion, octave, the track's transposition, its path, chord mode and modulation; its latched notes and chords, with their velocities; BALLSY's and BRICKLAYER's settings (BRICKLAYER's STUTTER and climbs too), BRICKLAYER's notes, and whether each plays; and its loops: which loops there are, where each stood against the others, which are taken out, whether they play, and their direction, speed, VARY, STUTTER and climbs. For the machine: the reverb, the delay, the scale, the root, the loops' transposition and REACT, SHADOW and ARP (on or off, the mode, the tracks taken in, the values on their pages). Not stored: the track chosen, MACRO and which page is up.

For example: record a loop and store snapshot 1; record an overdub and store snapshot 2. Snapshot 1 brings back the loop alone and snapshot 2 brings back both. Loops that are in both snapshots keep playing when you switch; a loop that comes back is placed where it stood against the others when it was stored.

A loop that a snapshot holds stays in memory even after you empty the looper (hold REC). It shares the looper's room with what you record: when the looper has no room left, REC says LOOPER FULL. Snapshots that share sounds, latched notes or loops store them once. If there is no room for a new snapshot, the screen says FULL; empty snapshots you no longer need (SHIFT + hold the pad).

Morph. With a morph time of 0 (OFF), a recalled snapshot is applied at once. With a longer time, the machine moves to it over that time; the snapshot's box and pad blink until it is reached:

  • Levels, pans, sends, filter, granulator, crush, distortion, the macros and envelope of a sound that stays, the modulation amounts, LFO rates and fades, the reverb's DECAY, DAMP and MIX, the delay's REPEATS, DAMP and MIX, and the sequencers' speed, rate, harmony and instability change gradually.
  • Everything that affects pitch changes at once, halfway through: scale, root, octaves and transpositions. So do the delay's TIME and the reverb's SIZE, the loops, the latched notes, chord mode, the sequencers and their notes, the loops' and BRICKLAYER's STUTTER and climbs, the modulation routings and LFO shapes, and REACT, SHADOW and ARP.
  • A track whose sound changes fades out from a quarter of the way, switches sound halfway and fades back in by three quarters.

Recalling another snapshot during a morph starts a new morph from the current state. The morph runs in the main loop and adds no load to the audio.

Snapshots are saved in the flash with the session (hold SAVE, off the SNAPSHOTS page, to save). A new session has none; sessions saved before BUILD 33 load with none.

Sessions

The keyboard always starts with no session loaded. There are 64 slots, numbered 1 to 64.

A session is the whole machine: every track's engine and its eight sounds with their macros and envelopes, its path, octave, level, pan, filter, granulator (and the character it was drawn with), crush, distortion, delay and reverb sends, modulation, chord mode, latched notes, BALLSY, BRICKLAYER, and its loops (playing or stopped, each overdub in or out, with their options and VARY); the scale and root, the moves along the scale, the delay, the reverb, REACT, SHADOW and ARP, the 16 snapshots with the loops they hold, the morph time, and the track chosen. A session stores in full the sound of the engine each track is on, and the others as the seed that made them and their level, so they come back the same.

Choosing and loading. Press SHIFT + SAVE: the SESSIONS page opens, on the session loaded if there is one. < and > step through the slots. The number is very large: red when the slot holds a session, grey with EMPTY under it when it does not; the session loaded says LOADED. Press SAVE:

  • on a slot holding a session, it loads (LOADING, then LOADED and the number);
  • on an empty slot, it starts a new session there (NEW and the number): a clean slate, as when the keyboard is switched on. The loops and latches go, every track is on its starting engine with new sounds and its settings at their defaults, and the scale, the delay, the reverb and the moves along the scale too. The session you were in stays saved as it was, and the next save goes to the new slot.

Either way the page closes. A track pad, or SHIFT + SAVE again, closes it without either.

Saving. Hold SAVE (0.8 s):

  • with a session loaded or chosen, it saves over it at once (SAVING, then SAVED and the number);
  • with none loaded or chosen (just after switching on), the first empty slot is offered (SAVE NEW): < and > choose NO or YES, SAVE answers (NOT SAVED on NO);
  • on the SESSIONS page, SAVE held saves into the slot shown, whatever is loaded: the session loaded is saved over at once; an empty slot asks SAVE NEW; another slot holding a session asks OVERWRITE? in red, on NO until > turns it to YES; SAVE answers.

The sessions live in the keyboard's user flash area: 40 sectors of 4 KB, shared with the presets, GLOBAL SETUP and the clipboard. A typical session takes one sector; a session with long loops takes more. When there is no room the screen says FULL. The first save takes over the area where the stock firmware kept its own settings; if you go back to the stock firmware, it rebuilds them.

A session also keeps the seeds its sounds were made from, with the path and the generation of the generators that drew them. Every generation is kept exactly as it was, so sessions and presets saved under an older build load with the same sounds after an update that brings new generators. Erasing flash silences the audio for a moment: a save uses blank flash when there is some, and the keyboard blanks free flash by itself while nothing sounds.

Backing up. The backup page saves them to a file on your computer and puts them back, over USB MIDI: it lists, sends and receives the sessions, the presets and GLOBAL SETUP, each record checked whole before it replaces the one with the same number. As each one arrives, the screen shows RESTORED and its number.

Global setup and MIDI

SHIFT + SAVE held (0.8 s) opens GLOBAL SETUP, the keyboard's own settings, kept apart from the sessions. It has two sections, MIDI and VELOCITY. < and > move through the entries and SAVE goes into one. On a setting, SAVE puts the focus on its value (a white field), < and > change it, and SAVE sets it; SHIFT + SAVE leaves it as it was, or goes back a level, and at the top level closes GLOBAL SETUP. Each level below the top starts with BACK. A track pad also closes it. What changed is written to the flash when you leave.

SectionPartSettingsAt the start
MIDIIN CHANTRACK 1 to 6: the channel each track listens to (OFF, 1–16); AUTO: the channel that plays the chosen track1 to 6; AUTO 16
OUT CHANTRACK 1 to 6: the channel each track sends on (OFF, 1–16)1 to 6
RECEIVENOTES, CC (ON / OFF)ON, ON
SENDNOTES, CC (ON / OFF)OFF, OFF
PORTSUSB IN; TRS OUT (the 3.5 mm jack, as MIDI OUT)ON, ON
VELOCITYKEYSCURVE: EVEN, SOFT (soft playing louder, for a light touch), HARD (for a firm touch), FIXEDEVEN
LOWEST, HIGHEST: the range the curve maps into (1–127)1, 127
FIXED: the velocity of every note when the curve is FIXED (1–127)100

MIDI in comes over USB only (the SMK-37 has no MIDI IN jack). A note plays every track whose IN channel it is on, and the chosen track on the AUTO channel, at its velocity (the VELOCITY settings apply to the keys only). The CCs a track answers to, on the same channels, and sends when SEND CC is on:

CCCC
7level74filter (64 off; below, low-pass; above, high-pass)
10pan91reverb send
16–19macros 1–4 of the track's sound92delay send
20–23macros 5–8 of the track's sound

MIDI out goes over USB and out of the TRS jack together: every message sent over USB also goes out of the jack, with or without a computer, while TRS OUT is ON. With SEND NOTES on, each track sends the notes it plays (from the keys, the loops, BALLSY, BRICKLAYER, REACT, SHADOW, ARP and MIDI in) on its OUT channel. With SEND CC on, the values above go out when they change, whatever changed them. Both are OFF at the start: turn them on to drive other instruments. A jack with nothing that answers is left quiet; the keyboard never waits on it. There is no MIDI clock, transport or program change: Tonitor has no tempo or patterns.

Modulation

Each track has a small modulation matrix: two LFOs and four slots that move the track's own values while it plays. The third press of SEQ opens the MOD page, in the track's colour. < and > go through its six entries (LFO 1, LFO 2, then MOD A to MOD D), and K3–K6 set the entry's four rows.

EntryK3K4K5K6
LFO 1, LFO 2SHAPE: SINE, TRI, SAW UP, SAW DN, SQUARE, STEPS (a new random value each cycle), DRIFT (a smooth random wander)RATE: 0.01 Hz (a cycle in 100 s) to 20 HzMODE: FREE (never restarted), NOTE (from the start at each note), ONCE (one cycle from each note, then held: an envelope)FADE: off, or in over up to 10 s from each note
MOD A – MOD DFROM: OFF, LFO 1, LFO 2, VELOCITY (softer notes less), KEY (the note, around C4), RANDOM (a new value each note)TO: the sound's eight macros (by their names), FILTER, GRAINS, CRUSH, DRIVE, REVERB, DELAY, LEVEL, PAN, LFO 1 RATE, LFO 2 RATEAMOUNT: −100 to +100 of the destination's whole swing(none: the row NOW shows what the slot does at the moment)

The modulation moves the values the track already has (what the knobs set, or the macros) around where they are, and the whole track follows. It moves a value once a block, so it costs next to nothing. Sessions keep each track's modulation, and copying a track copies it.

SHIFT + SEQ throws the chosen track's modulation anew (MOD RANDOM): both LFOs (any shape, rate, mode and fade) and two to four slots, from any source to any destination, by amounts that may go far. It takes risks on purpose; press it again for another, or set what you like on the MOD page.

HOME draws a modulation with some sounds, by engine and family: mostly with the slow, sustained families of FM, HIVE, BAYAREA and DRUID (a slow LFO on the tone, sometimes a fade in, sometimes a second, slower one in the stereo field or the reverb); now and then a struck or plucked sound gets its brightness on the velocity; never ANIMA or CALIGULA, whose sounds already move by themselves. A new sound with none clears the track's modulation; a preset loaded draws the same modulation again.

The filter and the crush

K3 is the chosen track's filter. From the middle (off), left is a resonant low-pass coming down from 20 kHz to about 35 Hz; right is a resonant high-pass going up from 16 Hz to about 12 kHz. The further from the middle, the more resonant. Its dial reads the mode and cutoff (LP 1.2 KHZ, HP 400 HZ, OFF).

K5 is the chosen track's crush. The middle is off. Left takes the bit depth down from 16 to 1.5 bits (the sound coarsens, then breaks up, quiet tails gating out); right takes the sample rate down from 44.1 kHz to about 300 Hz (metallic aliasing, then a stepped buzz). Both follow curves that keep the first half of the way playable; the rate glides, it does not jump. Its dial reads BITS 6.5 or RATE 2.6K. It comes after the granulator, before the track's limiter.

Both are saved with the session.

The granulator

K4 is the chosen track's granulator. The middle is off (as it starts).

  • Left, towards dark ambient: long, overlapping, slowly drifting grains (60–400 ms), pitched down now and then, reversed now and then, darkened, fed back on themselves, sometimes frozen (the buffer stops listening for a few seconds and the cloud turns over what it holds).
  • Right, towards scattering: short, fast grains (40 ms down to 4 ms, up to about 650 a second), their timing, place, pitch and level jittered more and more, reversed, stuttered, full of holes, decimated at the far end.

The further from the middle, the more grains and the less of the track. Its dial reads DARK 40, SCATTER 25 or OFF.

Each track keeps the last half second of its own sound (at 22.05 kHz, 8-bit μ-law: a little grit is part of it) and plays grains out of it, after its filter. Each track's granulator has a character of its own, drawn at random when the keyboard starts and every time a session is loaded: the intervals its grains are pitched to, how often they reverse, stutter, drop out or freeze, the shape of its scattered grains, how far its feedback and darkening go, how it drifts. The knob's position is saved with the session; the character is drawn anew. When the track's notes end, its grains ring on for about two seconds.

The distortion

K6 is the chosen track's distortion (0–100; 0 is off). It comes after the track's filter, granulator, crush and limiter, and before its level, pan and sends, so the delay and the reverb receive the distorted sound. Its dial reads DISTORTION n and the amount.

  • Two gain stages in series: the first symmetric (odd harmonics), the second asymmetric (even harmonics). The amount sets the drive into the first stage (×0.5 to ×32, up to +36 dB) and the second stage's gain and bias.
  • A bias in proportion to the input's own level is added before the first stage, so the clipped wave stays asymmetric and keeps its even harmonics at any drive. At low amounts the second harmonic dominates; higher amounts add more harmonics.
  • The highs are raised 6 dB before the stages and lowered 6 dB after, so the mids and highs distort more than the bass. The stages run at twice the sample rate to reduce aliasing. A low-pass after them goes from 16 kHz down to 6.5 kHz as the amount goes up.
  • The output level is matched to the dry signal's level (measured over about 0.2 s), so turning the amount up changes the drive and the harmonics, not the loudness.

Stored in sessions and copied with the track.

The delay

A master delay, mono, placed before the reverb. Each track's delay send (K7, its dial reading DELAY n / SEND) feeds it; its echoes go to both sides of the master, and half of their level also goes into the reverb, so the echoes are reverberated. Its line holds 2 seconds at 22.05 kHz in 8 bits (μ-law, as the granulator's), so the repeats are slightly dark and grainy.

The first press of SEQ opens the DELAY page: the title and its four values in rows, each with a bar.

KnobAt the start
K3TIME20 ms to 2 s, on a logarithmic scale (shown in ms). Turning it glides the delay over about 0.1 s, so the repeats bend in pitch rather than click65 (400 ms)
K4FEEDBACKhow much of each repeat comes back: 0 (one repeat) to 0.9540
K5DAMPa low-pass in the feedback path: each repeat darker than the one before40
K6MIXthe level of the echoes50

The delay's values and every track's send are kept in sessions; copying a track copies its send. The delay costs nothing while nothing goes into it and its tail has died away.

The reverb

A plate after Jon Dattorro (1997): a predelay, input diffusion, and a figure-of-eight tank whose two allpasses sweep slowly out of step, so the tail stays in motion and never rings. Each track sends to it after its level (K8, its dial reading REVERB n / SEND); the reverb's return is added to the mix before the master. The plate runs at 22.05 kHz, half the sample rate, with Dattorro's times and decay kept: its top is near 11 kHz.

The second press of SEQ opens the REVERB page.

KnobAt the start
K3SIZEthe room: every delay 0.5–1.25 times Dattorro's (turning it bends the tail, gently)70
K4DECAYthe time to fall 60 dB, 0.4 s to about 25 s, whatever the size65
K5DAMPhow fast the highs die in the tail40
K6MIXthe reverb's return level, ×0 to ×450 (×1)

The reverb's values are kept in sessions. It costs nothing while nothing goes into it and its tail has died away.

USB audio

Connected to a computer (or a phone or tablet that takes USB audio), the keyboard is also a USB audio input: choose "SMK-37 Tonitor" as the input in the recording program. It carries the master output, stereo, 16-bit, at 44.1 kHz (the rate Tonitor renders at; there is no 48 kHz). It is class compliant: no driver is needed, and MIDI goes on over the same cable. The stream is taken before fader 4, so the fader sets the headphones' level and not the recording's.

Voices and load

The six tracks are rendered a block of 32 samples (0.73 ms) at a time. Every sounding voice takes a share of that block. When the total passes 82 %, Tonitor protects the audio: it ends the quietest fading tails first, then the quietest voices, each faded over a few milliseconds so nothing clicks. A latched note is never ended this way. Below 82 % nothing is cut. What each engine costs, and how much you can stack, is measured in docs/smk37/engine-costs.md.

With all twelve voices busy, a new note takes the release tail that has rung longest (on any track), else the oldest note held on its own track, else the oldest held anywhere, never a latched one.

Every sound ends. Once its key is let go, a voice is faded out over 0.19 s when it has been 66 dB under its loudest for 0.2 s, when it has not fallen 1.5 dB in 2 s, or 30 s after its release began. Held and latched notes are not touched.

Starting, rescue and UBOOT

At power-on the screen shows TONITOR and the build (BUILD 31, for example), then the track view.

RESCUE. Hold OCTAVE− alone while switching the keyboard on: it starts in the rescue mode. The screen shows RESCUE, CONNECT USB, and RUN INSTALL (or UNKNOWN FLASH if it cannot read its flash). Connect it to the computer and run the installer: the rescue mode accepts a new package as the normal mode does. Nothing sounds and nothing is written in this mode until the installer writes. If Tonitor fails to start twice in a row, the keyboard starts in RESCUE by itself.

UBOOT. Hold OCTAVE− and OCTAVE+ together for 5 seconds while Tonitor runs: the audio stops, the screen shows UBOOT in blue, and the chip restarts into its own built-in updater (it appears on USB as WL82 UBOOT1.00). It is a way back whatever happens, and it is how the flash backup tool reads the keyboard (see docs/smk37/backup.md). Switch the keyboard off and on to leave it. Holding both buttons at power-on does not start RESCUE; hold them 5 seconds once Tonitor has started.

The engines

Each track plays one of eight engines, and keeps a sound of each. HOME draws a new sound on the track's engine, leaning to its path; SHIFT + HOME draws one of the same family; SHIFT + < / > draws one of the family before or after. Every sound is drawn from a seed, measured as it is made, and given the gain that brings it to one loudness. What each engine costs on the SMK-37's chip is in docs/smk37/engine-costs.md.

FM — six operators, DX7 style

The classic six-operator FM (msfa, the core of Dexed: 32 algorithms, rate/level envelopes, ratio or fixed frequencies, feedback, LFO, pitch envelope). FM plays from the shared pool of voices and is the lightest of the voiced engines. HOME draws a patch from one of the families of sound objects below.

FamilyAfter
METALbells and gongs: many carriers on inharmonic ratios, the high partials dying first
DRONEspectral drones: near-harmonic pairs detuned to beat, an index wandering over minutes
BRUITnoises: feedback and high ratios scattered by a sample-and-hold LFO
IMPACTstruck bodies of several kinds: thuds, wooden knocks, metal hits, drum skins, debris; the modulators dying before the carriers; the pitch falling to the note now and then
ITERATIFiterative objects: a sound pulsed by its own LFO, square or random
SPECTREa spectral arpeggio: rich tones a few cents apart whose beating lifts one harmonic after another
ABYSSsub-bass rumble folded by feedback, breathing slowly
FRICTIONcreaking: sub-audio fixed-frequency modulators and random pitch
CHOIRvowels: carriers on the harmonics nearest two formants, a late vibrato
BOWEDa bowed string: a saw from feedback, the bow's pressure rising with the swell
HOLLOWodd harmonics only: a dark pipe
BLOOMa tone that opens over seconds and half closes again
TIDEthree stacks crossfading, one fading as the next swells, under a slow tide of level
SHARDSa tone broken by random steps of pitch and chopped by a square
STATICring-modulated bands from modulators nailed to audio frequencies
WINDbreath and gusts over a soft drone
PLUCKplucked strings, bright or dark: the modulators die at once, the carriers die away, higher strings quicker
MALLETstruck bars (marimba, vibraphone, kalimba): a high modulator's knock, gone at once, the bar ringing on
WARPanything: ratios anywhere, partials nailed to frequencies, the pitch bent about by its envelope; now and then a long glide (with its siren), a pitch bouncing in at every note (up past it, back under, onto it), or both
GLITCHbroken, mechanical sounds: the level chopped by a square or random LFO, a crunch of heavy feedback with fixed-frequency modulators, the pitch thrown between steps, a slow uneven wobble
SHAPERa carrier nailed to 1–19 Hz under modulators that follow the key: the carrier hardly turns, so it works as a wave shaper, and the tone rolls over between its odd and even harmonics a few times a second, at the same pace up and down the keyboard
LADDERfour to six carriers on a ladder of ratios (near unison, an octave stack, uneven steps), their envelopes staggered: the partials enter one by one, or die one by one
REVERSEa sound that swells for as long as the key is held and stops when it is let go: tape run backwards
CREEPa held note leaving its pitch slowly, over seconds to tens of seconds
CLANGChowning's bells as the DX7's programmers made them: carriers turned by modulators on ratios off their harmonics, the index dying with the note

GLISSE (glissandi: a pitch envelope travelling octaves) and RUBBER (low ratios, the pitch bouncing in at every note) are no longer drawn: WARP took them over, with their weight. A sound saved as a GLISSE or RUBBER under an earlier generation still loads as it was; SHIFT + < / > steps over them.

SHAPER, LADDER, REVERSE, CREEP and CLANG were learned from a collection of 9,606 DX7 voices: the idioms its programmers used that the other families do not make. Each draws one of its family's skeletons (algorithm, feedback, every operator's frequency and level, taken from the collection), an envelope shape for each operator, and the rest within the family's ranges: new sounds of that kind, never one of the collection's voices again.

Each patch is then shaped with care: modulators on high ratios turned down (their sidebands alias and scream), the brightness scaled down the keyboard so high notes are not shrill nor low ones muddy, rate scaling on the carriers. A patch may also be made plucked whatever its family, have a modulator moved to another ratio, or an operator detuned against the rest, and about half the patches are bent once more, gently. HOME draws several patches, measures each, and keeps one whose brightness suits the track's path (darker on AMBIENT, brighter on EXPERIMENTAL), avoiding the family the track had.

On AMBIENT, FM favours DRONE, SPECTRE, CHOIR, BOWED, HOLLOW, TIDE, MALLET, LADDER, REVERSE and CREEP, draws WARP seldom, and never draws BRUIT, IMPACT, FRICTION, SHARDS, STATIC or GLITCH; then softer attacks, long tails, darker modulators, slow LFOs, no sirens, often an octave down. On EXPERIMENTAL it favours WARP most, then GLITCH, BRUIT, FRICTION, SHARDS, STATIC, SHAPER and CLANG, brighter and bent more often, and never draws SPECTRE, CHOIR, BOWED or TIDE.

Macros.

KnobMacro
K1BRIGHTNESSthe modulation index about 27 dB either way (down: towards pure sines; up: the feedback too), the carriers tilted (the higher partials up)
K2DETUNEthe carriers pulled apart ±40 cents and the modulators ±25 cents off them: beating, chorus, the partials off their places. INHARMONIC on METAL, BRUIT, IMPACT, ITERATIF, FRICTION, SHARDS, STATIC, WIND, WARP, GLITCH, MALLET and CLANG: every partial off its ratio (clangour)
K3SATURATIONfeedback and saturation turning up; a low-pass, smoother, turning down
K4MOTIONthe LFO's depths; turning up, a tremolo, quicker and deeper
K5ATTACKevery operator's first stage, 1/8 to 8 times as long
K6RELEASEevery operator's last stage once the key is up, 1/8 to 8 times as long
K7LFO RATEthe LFO 1/4 to 4 times as fast
K8VELOCITYabove the middle, the note's velocity on the brightness: soft darker, hard brighter, up to about 27 dB between the ends at full; at or below the middle, as drawn

ANIMA — a lo-fi synthesizer played by a simulated hand

ANIMA is the lo-fi engine: each voice runs at half the sample rate (22.05 kHz, so nothing above 11 kHz), its samples drawn out to the full rate by straight lines between them. Its pitches, rates and filters are scaled to sound where they would at the full rate; what goes is the top octave of air, and half of the chip's time.

A fixed-point port of the anima opcode from Vascular, rebuilt for Tonitor. While a key is held, a simulated finger rests on a virtual surface and drags one figure after another (orbits, figures of eight, scribbles, slow glides, now and then a flick), pressing in slow swells, and now and then lifting to land elsewhere. A ghost finger comes and goes on an irregular clock. Where the finger is, how hard it presses, how fast it moves and how long it has been down move the timbre, never the pitch.

The voice: two wavetable oscillators (24 band-limited single cycles), an FM pair, a stack of copies, a grain cloud, a filtered noise, a resonant filter, a wavetable tremolo; then the hand's chain: a downsampler, a waveshaper, a phaser, a second filter and a comb resonator tuned to the note. Each new sound is a design: which of these are in, on which waveforms, and for every parameter which gesture moves it, over what range, along what curve, plus a mod matrix of three to seven routes and Anima's eight sliders, drawn, often far from their middle.

Twenty-two kinds: HAZE, VOYAGE, GLASS, BELLS, GOLDEN (Anima's own) and BREATH, GRIT, SWARM, TIDE (waves of noise over a low drone), CHOIR (vowels, a formant the hand moves), SHARDS (glass grains scattered and crushed), BOWL (a beating inharmonic hum in a ringing comb), DUST (sparse crackle over a dark drone), MACHINE (a pulsing, folded mechanism), PLUCK (a burst through the comb tuned to the note, dying away), REED (nasal, through a formant the hand moves, a breath in it), FOG (a stack under fog, a slow phaser drifting through it), ORGAN (drawbars, a rotary tremolo, a little drive), BITS (pulses in few bits: the rate crushed and dragged about, folded), DRIFT (two saws drifting against each other, a chorus the hand moves), MURMUR (a dark cloud of noisy grains) and HOWL (noise through a resonance so sharp it whistles, swept by the hand).

The filter follows the keyboard, so low notes are not muffled nor high ones shrill; the second oscillator's interval suits the path (consonant on AMBIENT, anything on EXPERIMENTAL); and an AMBIENT sound nearly always has a resonant space to ring in. On AMBIENT, ANIMA draws mostly HAZE, GOLDEN, VOYAGE, TIDE, CHOIR, BOWL, FOG and DRIFT, never GRIT, SHARDS, MACHINE, BITS or HOWL, with a darker tone, more space, a slower hand, long releases and no crusher. On EXPERIMENTAL it draws mostly GRIT, SWARM, SHARDS, MACHINE, BITS and HOWL, never HAZE, TIDE, CHOIR, FOG or DRIFT, and makes them wild: the sliders near their tops, the resonance often screaming, a crushed sample rate, folding drive, a band of noise and scattered grains, often a fast tremolo, the comb ringing hard.

In Vascular a design plays up to six fingers, each a voice; here a voice has one finger on the sound. ANIMA plays from the shared pool of voices; PLUCK is the lightest kind, FOG and BREATH the heaviest.

Macros.

KnobMacro
K1TONEevery filter four octaves up or down (sharper when up), the FM brighter or darker
K2by kindwhat the kind is about, from nothing to far more: GRAINS, NOISE, FM (the index), FORMANT (sharper when up) or DRIVE (folded hard; turned down, a pure tone)
K3RESONATORmuch wetter and ringing longer (brought in if the sound had none), or dry
K4MOTIONthe hand four times quicker, a tremolo pulsing; or nearly still, no tremolo
K5ATTACK1/8 to 8 times as long
K6RELEASE1/8 to 8 times as long
K7GRAIN SIZEthe grains 1/4 to 4 times as long
K8PHASERdeeper and a little quicker (brought in if the sound had none), or shallower, gone at the bottom

CALIGULA — an organism

After the architecture of SOMA's LYRA-8 as Miguel Moreno's LIRA-8 emulates it (BSD licence), rebuilt for Tonitor and bent towards dark, restless textures. Eight oscillators in four pairs on two sides; each a triangle that its pair's sharpness pushes towards a square; each with a sensor and an envelope, slow (a long swell, a longer fall) or fast; each pair frequency-modulated at audio rate by its partner, the other pair of its side, a pair of the other side or the total feedback (the whole organism, saturated, fed back in). A hyper LFO of two LFOs (alone, AND, OR, XOR) opens and closes the modulation and gates chosen pairs into irregular rhythms; a short modulated delay (two lines, ~35 ms) choruses, flanges or warps it; a drive.

A CALIGULA track is played like the others: the keys play the scale's notes, and it is silent until a key is down. A key wakes the organism at that note; a second key on top moves the whole organism to the new note at once (a snap, not a glide), and letting go of it goes back to the key still held; letting go of the last key lifts the hand and the organism rings out. It is rooted: tuned around the note played, in intervals of it (octaves, fifths, unisons and semitone clusters that beat, tritones, the depths). The hyper LFO moves timbre, never pitch: no sirens. It is one organism a track, outside the pool of voices: its cost is the same whatever the number of notes.

Nobody touches the eight plates: a simulated hand does, while a key is held. Each species has its own hand: how often it touches, how long a finger stays, how many fingers at most, its favourite plates, quick taps against long holds. The first finger stays down until the key is let go, so the sound never drops out under a held key. Around the hand the organism has a life of its own: the modulation depths and the sharpness wander, oscillators fire in bursts at irregular times, and now and then the feedback and the drive surge for a moment. A pair's envelope may be slow: a swell of seconds, a release of up to nine seconds after the key is let go.

The hand often has a phrase: two to four plates it keeps coming back to, varied now and then, often on a pulse of its own (long, short, short, longer), so it plays like someone rather than like chance. HOME draws a new organism from ten species, tuned on one of ten sets of intervals (pillars of octaves and fifths, semitone clusters, the depths, the harmonics, unisons, tritones, fourths, a minor seventh, open fifths, a quarter-tone cluster):

Species
SPOREslow swells, held drones, breathing; low
THORNsharp, deep FM, driven, bursting often
HIVEthe hyper LFO quick and gating: irregular rhythms, bursts
CARRIONthe depths, heavy total feedback, the delay warped by the voices, surges
VEILmostly triangles, light modulation: the calmest
RUSTdriven, cross-modulated, surging, sometimes rhythmic
LITANYa slow choir: unisons and octaves beating, nothing sharp, a hand that stays
UNDERTOWdeep: heavy feedback and a warped delay pulling it under, slow surges
WIREhigh and sharp, clusters and quarter tones, a quick hand tapping, bursts
MOTHsoft triangles fluttering through the gates, on a pulse

On AMBIENT, CALIGULA draws SPORE, VEIL and LITANY most, then UNDERTOW, CARRION and MOTH, sometimes RUST; tuned on roots, fifths, octaves, depths and unisons; slow swells, softer edges, fewer bursts and surges, a slower hand. On EXPERIMENTAL it draws WIRE, THORN, HIVE and RUST most, never VEIL or LITANY; semitone clusters and tritones; sharper, more driven, more bursts and surges, a quicker hand.

Macros.

KnobMacro
K1WAVEFORMtriangles to squares
K2MOD DEPTHhow deeply the pairs modulate each other
K3FEEDBACKthe total feedback and the drive; DELAY (the delay's mix and feedback) for SPORE, VEIL, LITANY and MOTH
K4TOUCHEShow busy the hand is, its touches and bursts; GATE RATE (the hyper LFO's speed) for HIVE, MOTH and WIRE
K5ATTACKthe pairs' envelope attacks, 1/8 to 8 times as long
K6RELEASEthe pairs' envelope releases, 1/8 to 8 times as long
K7SPREADeach oscillator's detuning off its semitone, from none to twice
K8DELAY TIMEboth delay lines 1/4 to 4 times as long

RUSSOLO — noise, logic and broken buffers

RUSSOLO re-makes the techniques of Robert Heel's Noisferatu (GPL-3.0) in fixed point, for the keys. It runs at a third of the sample rate (about 14.7 kHz) in 10-bit values, each held until the next (the grit of a small DAC), then reduces its bits and holds its samples further as the sound says.

A RUSSOLO track is played like the others and is silent until a key is down: the key opens an envelope and sets the pitch (the oscillators' frequency, the speed a buffer is read at, the rate noise is sampled at); a second key on top moves it there at once; letting go of the last key lets it fade. Like CALIGULA it is one organism a track, outside the pool of voices; more notes cost nothing more. It is the lightest engine. HOME draws one of seventeen kinds:

Kind
HOLDsample-and-hold noise, its rate from the key
DUSTrandom clicks through a low-pass that follows the key
GATESnoise opened and closed by two triangles, one wandering off the other
CRACKLEsparse clicks ringing on short pitched decays, over hiss
NOR, XORtwo oscillators combined bit by bit
RINGtwo oscillators multiplied
CASCADEsquares modulating squares, a sub-octave below
CLANGtwo triangles at an inharmonic ratio, XOR'd; the ratio redrawn when two clocks meet
CHUNKSa generated buffer of noise, saw and silent chunks, read at the key's speed and rebuilt in parts
JUMPthe buffer read with jumps at random
WANDERa window wandering through the buffer
BENDan address bit of the buffer forced to 0 or 1, flipped or held; which and how change on a clock
QUADfour such bendings at once, each switched on and off by chance
BLIPSdecaying triangles fired by chance on the key's harmonics
WALKa random walk over a scale's steps from the key
CHORDtriangles on the key (minor, major, open fifths or suspended), slowly beating and swelling

Its level is measured when it is drawn, and never raised so far that its loudest click could clip. On AMBIENT, RUSSOLO draws CHORD most, then DUST, CRACKLE, BLIPS, WALK and WANDER, never the logic kinds (NOR, XOR, RING, CASCADE, CLANG), JUMP, BEND or QUAD; clean (9–10 bits), slow attacks, long releases, calmer chance, no major chords. On EXPERIMENTAL it draws NOR, XOR, CLANG, BEND and QUAD most, never WALK or CHORD; crushed to 4–9 bits, often sample-held, abrupt attacks and short releases, chance driving it hard.

Macros.

KnobMacro
K1the kind's first parameternamed for what it does: RATE, TONE, WIDTH, HISS, RATIO, SPREAD, DENSITY, …
K2the kind's second parameterCHANCE, DENSITY, WANDER, DRIFT, SUB, CLOCK, CHANGE, …
K3CRUSHfewer bits and longer sample holds, or cleaner
K4RANDOMNESShow much chance drives it; above the middle, stutters too (its sample frozen a moment)
K5ATTACK1/8 to 8 times as long
K6RELEASE1/8 to 8 times as long
K7CHORDon the CHORD kind, the chord moved up to three types away (minor, major, open fifths, suspended)
K8HOLDeach sample held longer, or shorter

DRUID — strings and resonant bodies

DRUID is a fixed-point port of the resonators of Mutable Instruments Rings by Émilie Gillet (MIT licence). It plays from the shared pool of voices. Each kind is one of Rings' resonators and an exciter:

Resonator
Stringa Karplus-Strong string: a delay line read with Hermite interpolation, damped by a short FIR filter (brightness) and a state-variable low-pass, its decay set as a time to −60 dB. Dispersion (STRUCTURE) stretches the partials with an all-pass stage, adds noise to the period near the top, or below a quarter of the range bends the bridge so the string buzzes. The output is picked up at the position along the string
Sympathetic stringsa string and three more tuned to intervals of its note (octaves, fifths, a twelfth, chosen by STRUCTURE), driven only by the first string's sound; their pickup positions drift slowly
Modalup to 16 two-pole resonators at the partials of a bar or plate, stretched or squeezed by STRUCTURE; each partial's level depends on the position
Exciter
PluckRings' plucker: a burst of noise as long as the position's share of the period, through a comb filter and a low-pass
Strikea short pulse, longer and softer as the brightness goes down
Bownoise for as long as the key is held, swelling in and dying away when released
Dustrandom impacts for as long as the key is held
KindResonatorExciter
PLUCKstringpluck
BOWEDstringbow
STRUCKstring, stretched partialsstrike
SITARstring, buzzing bridgepluck
RATTLEstringdust
HARPsympathetic stringspluck
DRONEsympathetic stringsbow
BELLmodalstrike
BOWLmodalbow
PLATEmodaldust

On AMBIENT, DRUID favours BOWED, HARP, DRONE, BELL and BOWL, with long decays that carry on after the key is released. On EXPERIMENTAL it favours RATTLE and PLATE, with shorter decays, faster dust, extreme positions and a stronger damping when the key is released. Releasing a key damps the sound by an amount set per sound, from ringing on to stopping short. Each voice's delay lines are 16-bit and use the memory an ANIMA voice would use: a string reaches down to about 29 Hz, and sympathetic strings that would not fit their shorter lines are tuned an octave up. HARP and DRONE (a string with three sympathetic strings) are the heaviest sounds of all the engines.
